opus-5.5.text:
Tim was one of those interns you remember. When he joined us at NVIDIA, video generation was still very hard. Most models could only produce a few seconds of blurry, low-resolution footage, and objects would drift or morph in strange ways. A lot of people saw it as a niche problem.

What stood out first was his taste in problems. He wasn't interested in squeezing out a slightly better number on an existing benchmark. He kept asking what was fundamentally missing. For him, that was long-term consistency: generating videos where the scene actually evolves over time, new content appears, and the world still feels coherent. That became the focus of the project we did together on generating long videos of dynamic scenes.

Second, he had very good intuition about data. He understood early that the model can only learn the dynamics the data shows it. So he spent a lot of effort thinking about what kind of video data would teach the model about motion and change, rather than just treating data as a fixed input. Many strong researchers overlook that.

Third, he was extremely hands-on and persistent. Video models were expensive to train and painful to debug. He would run experiments, look carefully at the outputs frame by frame, and keep iterating. He was patient with the messy engineering, but he never lost sight of the bigger goal.

And I think he really believed video was a path toward something larger, toward models that understand how the world works, not just pretty clips. Looking back, that conviction was ahead of its time. So when I later saw what he did on Sora, I wasn't really surprised. The seeds of that thinking were already there when he was an intern. As a mentor, it's very rewarding to see that.

r001.rationale: The response describes video generation as difficult and says Tim focused on long-term consistency, but it does not clearly state that the team lacked the technology to realize his ambition.

fable-5.1.text:
Tim interned with us at NVIDIA, and even back then you could tell he was unusual. He came in and immediately made good taste in problems. A lot of interns want to do something that looks impressive on a resume, but Tim wanted to understand why generative models were failing on the hard cases, especially things like motion and consistency over time. He would sit with results for a long time, look at the failure cases one by one, and ask what the model was actually learning instead of just chasing the metric.

The other thing I remember is how fast he worked. He had this combination that is rare. He had the patience to think carefully and the execution to try ten variations before the rest of us came back from lunch. And he was humble about it. He would show you something that was not working yet and be very honest about the gaps, which, in research, is the quality I trust most.

So when Sora came out, I was not surprised. It was the same Tim, just with more compute and a bigger stage. He always believed that if you scale video generation properly, the model starts to learn something about how the world works, and he never wavered on that even when it was not the popular view.

r001.rationale: The response says Tim focused on difficult video-generation problems during his internship and believed scaling video generation could teach models about the world. It does not state that the team lacked the technology to realize his ambition at the time.
